title: CORS: how browsers let one website call another
subject: cs

questions.question: Which change turns a URL into a different origin?
questions.explanation: An origin is scheme + domain + port, so changing the scheme changes the origin. The path (A) is not part of the origin.

questions.question: The browser rule that a page may only read responses from its own origin is called the _____ policy.
questions.explanation: It is the default; CORS is the way a server relaxes it for chosen sites.

questions.question: Why do browsers have the same-origin policy at all?
questions.answer: To protect users: without it, any page you visit could use your logged-in browser to read your data from other sites, like your bank or email.
questions.explanation: The policy stops one site from silently reading another site's answers through your browser.

questions.question: Is it true that the server is the one that blocks a cross-origin request when CORS fails?
questions.explanation: The server only sends (or doesn't send) permission headers. The browser reads them and blocks the page from getting the reply.

questions.question: What is a preflight request?
options: A request that logs the user in first
An OPTIONS request the browser sends first to ask if the real request is allowed
A request the server sends to the browser before loading a page
A copy of the request kept in case the first one fails
questions.explanation: Before a non-simple request (like a POST with JSON), the browser asks permission with OPTIONS. It has nothing to do with logging in (A).

questions.question: Is it true that every cross-origin request starts with a preflight?
questions.explanation: Simple requests, like a plain GET with no special headers, are sent directly. The browser still checks the Allow-Origin header on the reply.

questions.question: The server names the origin allowed to read its reply in the _____ header.
questions.explanation: If it is missing or names another origin, the browser hides the reply from the page.

questions.question: If the allowed origin is set to the wrong address, what happens when the real site calls the API?
options: The request works, CORS is only a warning
The browser blocks the call, even though the server works
questions.explanation: The server answers normally but without a matching Allow-Origin header, so the browser refuses. This is exactly what can happen with a wrong deployment address.

questions.question: Why can curl call an API that the browser blocks with a CORS error?
questions.answer: CORS is enforced by browsers only. curl is not a browser, so it never checks the Allow-Origin header and simply shows the reply.
questions.explanation: The permission check lives in the browser, not on the server, so any non-browser client skips it.

questions.question: Is it true that CORS stops attackers from sending requests to your API?
questions.explanation: Anyone can call the API with curl or a script. Real protection needs input validation, rate limits or authentication on the server.
